title: The Quiet Indian Who Ran the World Bank's Economic Brain Is Calling It a Day
excerpt: Indermit Gill's retirement as chief economist leaves a vacancy at the top of global development thinking — and a legacy that includes fixing the institution's biggest data scandal
body:
An internal memo at the World Bank confirmed this week what Washington's development policy circles had been anticipating for months: Indermit Gill, the institution's chief economist and senior vice president for development economics, will retire in August 2026. His departure marks the end of a tenure that was defined less by headline-making pronouncements than by the painstaking institutional repair work that followed one of the Bank's most embarrassing episodes.

Gill, who is Indian-born and spent much of his career shuttling between Washington, Delhi, and various emerging-market postings, took the top economics job at a particularly fraught moment. The Bank's flagship Doing Business report had been discontinued in 2021 after an investigation revealed that senior officials had manipulated data to favour China and Saudi Arabia — a scandal that damaged the institution's credibility as an arbiter of economic governance. Gill was tasked with building a replacement.

The result was Business Ready, a new assessment framework designed with greater methodological transparency and external peer review. It was not a glamorous assignment. Redesigning a global benchmarking tool that governments and investors rely on is the kind of work that earns respect from wonks and indifference from everyone else. But it was essential, and by most accounts, Gill executed it competently.

## The Policy Record

Beyond the data infrastructure work, Gill's tenure coincided with a cascade of global economic disruptions that tested the Bank's analytical capacity. The Iran war's impact on oil markets, persistent inflation in emerging economies, and slowing growth across sub-Saharan Africa all demanded real-time analysis from the Bank's economics division. The institution's Global Economic Prospects reports under Gill were notably more candid about downside risks than their predecessors — a shift that earned some praise from academics and occasional irritation from the Bank's operational teams, who prefer optimism when pitching lending programmes.

Gill also deepened the Bank's engagement with think tanks in Rome and Tokyo, building policy partnerships that extended the institution's intellectual reach beyond its traditional Washington-London axis. His focus on debt transparency for low- and middle-income countries produced practical tools that helped several governments renegotiate terms with creditors, though critics argue the Bank's influence on actual debt outcomes remains marginal.

## The Indian Thread

Gill's retirement creates an interesting vacancy in the constellation of Indian-origin figures who currently occupy senior positions in global economic governance. Ajay Banga, another Indian-born executive, has led the World Bank as president since 2023. Gita Gopinath serves as first deputy managing director at the International Monetary Fund, where the chief economist position is also now vacant following a separate departure announced this summer.

The concentration of Indian-origin talent at the apex of Bretton Woods institutions is not accidental. It reflects decades of elite Indian education in economics — the Delhi School, the Indian Statistical Institute, JNU — feeding into American doctoral programmes and then into the multilateral system. Gill himself is a product of this pipeline, having studied at the University of Chicago before joining the Bank.

For the Indian diaspora, these appointments carry symbolic weight that transcends their policy impact. They represent a particular kind of diasporic achievement: not the flashy tech-billionaire variety, but the quieter, more institutional kind — the sort that shapes how the world measures poverty, allocates development capital, and thinks about economic growth.

## What Comes Next

The Bank has indicated it will begin a successor search soon, though no timeline has been specified. The role requires someone who can navigate both academic rigour and institutional politics — a combination that narrows the field considerably. The simultaneous vacancy at the IMF adds competitive pressure, as the same pool of elite economists is likely to be courted for both positions.

Gill leaves behind an institution that is somewhat better equipped to produce credible economic analysis than the one he inherited, but one that still faces structural questions about its relevance in a world where development finance is increasingly shaped by China's Belt and Road lending and private capital flows that dwarf multilateral commitments.

His legacy, like much of his career, will be assessed in the language of institutional plumbing rather than grand strategy. In the world of global development, that may be the most honest kind of contribution there is.
